$note: SHARED PARITY FIXTURE — read by BOTH `cargo test` (src-tauri/tests/adapter_parity_fixture.rs) and `pnpm test` (src/platform/adapter-parity.test.ts). It pins the SEMANTICS of the settings_put_provider derivation across the two implementations: the Rust host in src-tauri/crates/vela-settings, and the hand-written mirror of it in src/platform/browser-adapter.ts. The Rust host is the specification: when the two disagree, the fake is wrong (docs/architecture/conventions.md §8).
$howToChange: Never edit an expectation to make a suite pass. Change the host first, re-derive the expectation from the host's behaviour, then make the fake match. A case whose expectation was edited to match the fake proves nothing.

cases.why: THE case Vela exists for: llama.cpp on 127.0.0.1 over http with no key. Must raise nothing at all, or the product nags people for using local models correctly.
llama.cpp started with --api-key. The credential never leaves the machine, so it is not a concern.
Header names are normalised host-side (HTTP/2 requires lowercase); the fake must normalise identically.
A fully-qualified `LocalHost.` is still loopback: the host lowercases and strips trailing dots.
`127.1` is a legal IPv4 shorthand. Both sides must run it through a URL parser, not a string match.
`0x7f.0.0.1` is 127.0.0.1 after WHATWG IPv4 parsing.
`2130706433` is 127.0.0.1 as a single decimal.
127.0.0.2 is loopback (the whole /8 is), and a Required credential that is not stored is a notice, never a traffic risk.
The query-string concern is deliberately silent on loopback: a key logged by the user's own llama.cpp, on the user's own machine, has not gone anywhere.
`*.localhost` resolves to loopback by RFC 6761 and the host treats it so.
Neither side strips userinfo from the echoed baseUrl. Pinned so that if one side ever starts sanitising it, the other is forced to as well.
A bare authority gains a `/` path in the echoed URL.
A pasted URL carries whitespace. Both sides trim before parsing.
The echoed URL is the canonical serialisation, not the input text.
The endpoint is echoed whole; neither side quietly drops a query string a runtime may need.
A GPU box on the LAN over plaintext: the conversation is readable by every hop, and anyone on the LAN can use the model.
The credential itself crosses the wire in the clear. Highest level, and the concern order is the host's enum order, not alphabetical.
Nothing is transmitted, so credential exposure is absent even though traffic exposure remains.
Top of the RFC1918 172.16/12 range, encrypted: only the open-endpoint notice remains.
fc00::/7 unique-local addresses are LAN addresses.
fe80::/10 link-local, with the query-parameter auth mode: the key crosses the wire in a URL.
IPv4 link-local is a local-network address, not a public one.
0.0.0.0 is the unspecified address. It is NOT loopback — treating it as loopback would silence the warning for an endpoint that can route anywhere.
0.1.2.3 is public: the host compares against the single unspecified address, not the 0.0.0.0/8 block, so an implementation that tests the first octet alone diverges here.
`[::]` is the IPv6 unspecified address and the host classifies it alongside 0.0.0.0.
A LAN box over TLS with a stored key: leaves the device, but nothing is exposed.
`gpu-box.local..` — the host strips ALL trailing dots before matching the suffix, so this is still a LAN name. A single-dot strip would misclassify it as public.
`.internal` is a private-use suffix.
The ordinary hosted-API configuration. Leaves the device and is still level none.
The only failure state in the whole auth model.
Plaintext to the public internet with a real key: both traffic and credential are exposed.
Two independent concerns that are not the credential-exposure one: level stays elevated.
Encrypted, but open to anyone who can route to it.
A routable IPv4 literal is public, not private.
172.32.0.1 is one block past the private range. An off-by-one in either implementation shows here.
fec0::/10 is deprecated site-local, outside fc00::/7 and fe80::/10, so the host calls it public.
:443 on https is the default and disappears from the canonical form.
A non-default port survives normalisation, and the api-key header mode reaches the same credential-exposure verdict as bearer.
Case normalisation is host-and-scheme only. A fake that lowercases the whole URL breaks paths.
The trailing dot is stripped for classification but kept in the echoed URL.
IDNA happens in the parser, so both sides must show the same ASCII host.
`localhost.localdomain` is a real DNS name. Only `localhost` and `*.localhost` are loopback.
Substring matching on `localhost` would silence the warning for an attacker-chosen host.
`::ffff:127.0.0.1` is an IPv6 address whose Rust is_loopback() is false. Pinned as the host's behaviour: it is warned about rather than silently trusted.
Same rule for a mapped LAN address: classified public, i.e. the louder side of the ambiguity.
ADVERSARIAL: `127.evil.example` is a DNS name an attacker can register. Prefix-matching `127.` would report a remote endpoint as loopback and hide every warning.
ADVERSARIAL: `10.example.test` is a domain, not an RFC1918 address.
ADVERSARIAL: the same trap for the 192.168 prefix.
ADVERSARIAL: the same trap for the 172.16/12 prefix.
ADVERSARIAL: the same trap for the link-local prefix.
ADVERSARIAL: a hex-prefix test applied to a DNS name would call `fdn.example.test` a ULA address.
ADVERSARIAL: `feasible.example.test` starts with `fea`.
`http:///v1` yields host `v1` in both URL parsers. Pinned as a known shared quirk: if either side ever starts rejecting it, the other must too.
A key in the store for a provider configured to send nothing is NOT 'present': the endpoint is still unauthenticated, and the UI must not claim otherwise.
requirement=required with mode=none can never be satisfied. Both concerns fire and the provider is unusable — no crash, no silent repair.
Query parameter names are case-sensitive, unlike header names. Note the level: https does not clear the query-string concern, because TLS does not stop the server writing the URL to a log.
`AUTHORIZATION` becomes `authorization`.
The --api-key-not-set case: configured mode, empty store, and nothing to warn about.
Only http and https reach a model endpoint.
A file: URL would turn a settings row into a local-file read primitive.
data: URLs are not endpoints.
javascript: must never survive parsing.
Free text is not an endpoint.
Whitespace only: the shortest way to describe no endpoint at all.
`http://` has no host to send anything to.
`//host/path` has no scheme, so it cannot be classified.
65535 is the maximum port.
`1.2.3.999` is a failed IPv4 parse, not a domain.
A zone id is not accepted by either URL parser.
An API-key header must be named, or the credential goes nowhere.
Same rule for the query-parameter mode.
The id namespaces the keychain entry.
`/` separates provider from field in a keychain key.
Every provider needs a name the user can see.
The id is a settings key and a keychain entry name; the host caps it at 200 characters.
The same 200-character ceiling applies to the label the user types.
Two faults at once: the host binds auth before parsing the URL, so `header` is the reported field. Pins the validation ORDER, not just the outcome.
Two faults at once: the URL is parsed before the id is validated.
